scenarios.explanation:
1. An address finds a computer; a port finds an application
The IP address chooses a host. A destination port chooses a listening application on that host. The sender also has a source port, which lets the reply return to the right conversation. A listener must match the transport protocol as well as the port number.

2. TCP opens a two-way conversation
A client sends SYN (a request to start). A listening server returns SYN-ACK (its opening reply), reversing both address and port pairs. The client sends ACK (an acknowledgement). Only after both peers have opened the connection can this activity send its report. TCP provides an ordered byte stream in real systems; this small model demonstrates the opening and one supplied fragment, not retransmission or congestion control.

3. UDP sends a datagram directly
UDP does not use the TCP handshake. The sensor sends one supplied datagram. The trace distinguishes sending, delivery to a host and receipt by a matching UDP listener. No reply or successful delivery is guaranteed by UDP itself.

4. Worked pairing with different practice values
In the separate practice network, report clients target TCP 8088 but the TCP listener starts on 8089. Set the TCP listener to 8088, then Check configuration: both reports can open and deliver. UDP 8088 is a different listener, so it can receive the sensor datagram at the same numeric port. Another valid repair is to point both report clients at TCP 8089. Changing only one report leaves partial completion.

No real sockets/network/host commands, retransmission, sequence numbers, congestion, data ACK, close/reset, wildcard binding, IPv6/NAT or complete TCP implementation. Activity ports 1–65535; UDP source zero is excluded here, not declared universally invalid.

scenarios.objective:
Restore both TCP report conversations to Server service 8443, including the return SYN-ACK and received report content.

Keep the UDP sensor service 9555 working. Keep maintenance-forward, unsolicited-datagram and other-service blocked at the named office policy boundary.

Edit only R1’s ACL document. Keep all endpoint settings and the supplied routes intact. Use Check configuration and inspect every exchange, not only the first successful packet.

scenarios.explanation:
1. Read the opening in both directions
A TCP SYN travels from the client’s high source port to the server’s service port. SYN-ACK travels from that service port back to the original client port. Forward delivery alone cannot establish a TCP connection. Look at the actual packet pairs in the trace before editing a rule.

2. Read an ordered ACL rule
In the supplied extended ACL document, a port after the first address matches the source port; a port after the second address matches the destination port. Rules are evaluated in sequence order, first match wins. interface office with ip access-group RETURN out applies as packets leave the router toward the client. The matching syntax is a bounded IOS-style subset; the editor does not execute equipment commands.

3. Worked reverse rule with different practice values
The practice reports use service 8088 and client ports 50123/50124. Their SYN-ACK packets have source 8088 and those high destination ports. A reverse permit matching destination 8088 is therefore on the wrong side. Match source 8088 and destination range 49152–65535 for the supplied server/client hosts. Keep FORWARD in place and the final deny so unsolicited traffic remains blocked.

4. Verify useful work and preserved restrictions
Check configuration sends two independent report conversations, a UDP sensor datagram and three forbidden probes. A missing listener does not prove an ACL restriction. Allowing everything fixes a report but fails the protected probes; blocking everything fails the report. This finite roster verifies stated behavior rather than every possible network flow.
